positive.query: Repurpose our approved research report into Instagram and LinkedIn posts plus a newsletter section, and tell me which ones need review again.
Turn last month's webinar recording into talking points, a blog post, and captioned clips without changing what the speakers actually said.
Adapt our annual report into a partner kit that corporate partners can post, keeping every statistic tied to its source.

nearMiss.query: I have a rough idea about burnout among nonprofit staff. Write me a LinkedIn post about it.
Draft this month's full newsletter issue with a program update, an event announcement, and a donor thank-you.
Write an original blog post on five ways families can talk about stress at home. We have no source material yet.

holdout.query: Cut down our approved workshop deck into a parent email and one summary slide, and flag any adaptation that adds a claim.

scenarios.task: Our research team published an approved report on a hypothetical poll of 800 college students at four partner campuses, fielded in spring. It was approved for campus partners and funders. Findings: 38 percent said they had skipped class in the past month because of stress; 61 percent said they would know where to find help on campus; students who had attended a peer workshop were more likely to say they would reach out to a friend who was struggling (the report notes there was no comparison group). The executive director wants an Instagram carousel, a LinkedIn post, a two-paragraph newsletter section for parents of high school students, and copy a corporate partner's employee resource group can post internally. She suggested this headline for everything: 'Nearly 4 in 10 young people are skipping school because of stress, and our workshops fix that.' Draft the pieces and tell us which ones the content owner has to look at again.
scenarios.baselineFailure: A generic answer drafts the pieces, lightly softens the headline, and says everything should be reviewed, without tracing each sentence to a numbered source claim, without noticing that parents of high schoolers and a corporate partner's employees are audiences outside the approval, and without stating which specific change triggers which level of review.
